results.title: Tesla Full Self-Driving v15: a first-hand look at Reality View, new features
results.content:
FSD still struggles with parking, it has routine bugs from update to update, it does not recognize potholes or large bumps on the road, speed control is a common complaint, and Navigation has been one of the biggest pain points.

However, v15 will likely bring massive improvements to capability and give people more options, like potentially parking orientation and more refined spot selection. We can only wait and see what Tesla will include.

results.title: Tesla launches FSD v15, targets its biggest weaknesses, from signs to potholes | Electrek
results.content:
The driving side is harder to judge. Tesla is going straight at the weaknesses that owners and regulators complain about most: misread speed limits, potholes, school zones, debris. If v15 delivers real progress on all of those, it’s a really good update.

But “improved detection” doesn’t tell us how much better, and a 25x multiplier without the underlying number is hard to check. FSD has gone two steps forward, one step back throughout its history, with point releases regularly breaking things the previous version handled fine. And Tesla still won’t publish the disengagement data that would settle it. [...] Signs are a big one. In a test published in September, Brussels nonprofit Johanna.be found that FSD exceeded the limit in 55% of the 30 km/h zones it drove through, averaging 44 km/h. In most of those zones, the car’s screen showed a 50 km/h limit. It didn’t read the sign.

Potholes are another. In August, Musk said pothole avoidance was “coming soon”, something he had already promised back in 2019. Today, FSD still drives straight through them. [...] School zones are on the list too. NHTSA is reviewing a petition claiming Tesla’s Robotaxis speed through active school zones, on top of an investigation it opened in October 2025 into FSD traffic-law violations like running red lights. Slowing for speed cameras fits the same theme, though it also suggests Tesla is fine with FSD going over the limit when there’s no camera around.

So if v15 really fixes these, it’s a very good update. The question is by how much.

One change goes the other way. Tesla says it is “decreasing strictness” of driver monitoring in higher-speed driver profiles, at a time when sleeping drivers on FSD keep making headlines and Tesla is tightening monitoring in Europe at regulators’ request.

## The “25x” is the critical intervention rate

results.title: Tesla FSD v15 - an honest patch for half a decade of real-world failures - ArenaEV
results.content:
Almost every bullet point in the v15 release notes targets a localized failure point owners have complained about for years. Sign detection is a prime example. Back in September, the Brussels-based nonprofit Johanna.be tested FSD through 30 km/h zones and found the system breached the limit 55 percent of the time, averaging 44 km/h. The center screen stubbornly displayed a 50 km/h limit. It simply wasn't reading the signs. The v15 notes claim improved detection of signs, small animals, road debris, and chains. It explicitly mentions better speed handling in school zones. This is incredibly timely given the NHTSA opened a formal investigation in October 2025 into FSD running red lights and speeding through active school zones. But the new speed camera detection logic is deeply cynical. If [...] # Tesla FSD v15 - an honest patch for half a decade of real-world failures

Tesla dropped the release notes for Full Self-Driving v15 on X, and reading them feels less like a step into the future and more like a brutally honest confession of everything the system got wrong until now. Potholes. Speed limits. School zones. These aren't edge cases in a simulated silicon sandbox - they're the daily realities of commuting, and for years, FSD has treated them with alarming indifference. The update promises a 25x improvement in critical intervention rates and a heavily hyped Reality View interface. But the real story is that Tesla is finally forcing its multi-billion-dollar neural net to look down at the broken roads we drive on. [...] We've been here before with Tesla software updates. Every major version ships with tons of hype, followed by a period of regression, before eventually settling into genuine improvement. When v14 launched in October 2025, it arrived loaded with hallucinations, erratic brake stabbing, and aggressive speeding. Early crowdsourced data showed it managed a dismal 1,178 km between critical disengagements - well below the internal targets. It took seven months and a long string of point releases to get that software to a point where owners weren't fighting the steering wheel. FSD doesn't improve in a straight line. It stumbles backward just as often as it leaps forward - the good old “two steps forward, one step back” scenario.

results.title: Tesla launches FSD v15, targets its biggest weaknesses, from signs to potholes | Hacker News
results.content:
Beyond the amazing enhanced visuals, V15 looks set to fix most of my biggest annoyances with FSD. Right now, it speeds through school zones unless I take over, even when the nav has detected a speed camera. Since I live and work in buildings with underground garages, I also notice how poorly it handles that very common parking situation. And it plows straight over speed bumps and other road imperfections, to the point where I wonder whether I should take over just to avoid them. Overall I’m still amazed with how good FSD is in most driving situations, and typically feel safer with it in control. [...] |  |  |  |
